To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pioneer herbaceous species that colonize the burnt soil are able to retain the post-fire pulse in the burnt soil and to provide it to pine seedlings, and that the pioneer herbaceous cover also reduces N loss from the burnt soil, thus providing indirect benefits for tree N nutrition.

the N pulse released by the fire was successfully kept in a burnt soil-plant ecosystem through its uptake by pioneer herbaceous species, and that the pine seedlings were able to take up a significant proportion of this N pulse during the 2-year period.
(1) the pioneer species can efficiently capture the post-fire pulse inorganic-N and (2) this N is available for the trees in the medium-term, although it is assimilated at a lower rate than expected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of pioneer species on the N cycling in burnt soils.
the availability of N in a burnt soil and the transfer of N from a pioneer plant species to a tree species.
the role of pioneer herbaceous plants in the N economy of burnt soils.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the N uptake by the herbaceous plants after the fire is a very important factor to consider in order to understand N dynamics and N nutrition by trees in the first post-fire year.
the N derived from the pioneer herbaceous plants is available to pine seedlings during at least 2 years after the fire.
the post-fire pulse is not only available in the short term (as is generally assumed) but also for the medium and possibly long term.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pioneer herbaceous cover is a key component of the post-fire recovery process, as it provides a temporary N sink for the soil, which is essential to maintain N availability for the tree seedlings.
the pioneer herbaceous plants are a major component in the recovery process of burnt soils, and the establishment of a herb cover is a prerequisite for a successful post-fire reforestation.
pioneer herbaceous plants are important for tree nutrition in post-fire succession.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the post-fire increase in available N in burnt soil can be used by pine seedlings, which is a positive factor for the establishment of the tree layer.
the N pulse provided by a post-fire herbaceous cover can be a valuable resource for trees in the short term.
the pioneer herbaceous plants can play an essential role as a source of N to trees in the medium and long term after a fire.
